reviews.scope: equivalence-preserving equation manipulation during elimination
reviews.reason: Both affine substitution and shared-term elimination rely on adding, subtracting, or scaling equations by nonzero quantities so that derived one-variable conditions preserve the original solution set without dividing by zero.

reviews.scope: expand an affine substitution in a quadratic expression
reviews.reason: Substituting a two-term affine expression for one variable into quadratic or product terms requires expanding products of polynomials to collect coefficients and determine the resulting single-variable equation degree.
reviews.counterexample: Systems sharing an identical squared term such as y^2 can be reduced by direct replacement or equation subtraction without expanding polynomial products.

reviews.scope: recover a real variable from its squared value
reviews.reason: When elimination leaves a condition on a squared variable, recovering admissible real solutions requires rejecting negative squared values and taking both positive and negative real square roots when positive.
reviews.counterexample: When an affine substitution reduces the system to a factorable quadratic, the second variable is recovered linearly from the affine relation without taking square roots.

reviews.scope: substitution strategy transferred from linear systems
reviews.reason: Isolating one variable and substituting into the other equation transfers the elimination strategy learned for linear systems, even though the resulting single-variable equation here may be quadratic rather than linear.
reviews.counterexample: One can eliminate a shared squared expression directly between two quadratic equations without isolating a linear variable as in linear-system substitution.

reviews.scope: four sides and diagonals of a simple quadrilateral
reviews.reason: Understanding what it means for four positive lengths to form a closed simple quadrilateral and what a diagonal is depends on foundational polygon concepts, excluding the diagonal-counting formula.

reviews.scope: choose a diagonal making two nondegenerate triangles
reviews.reason: Proving sufficiency by splitting the quadrilateral along a shared diagonal requires triangle side inequalities to bound an admissible diagonal length that simultaneously forms two nondegenerate triangles with the given sides.
reviews.counterexample: Checking necessity or feasibility directly via the four-side inequality that the longest side is strictly less than the sum of the other three avoids explicit triangle-pair construction.

reviews.scope: universal and existential quantifier meanings in inference
reviews.reason: Determining whether premises entail a conclusion or constructing a countermodel requires interpreting universal rules as applying to every domain member and existential claims as asserting at least one witness.

reviews.scope: represent universal inclusion premises as subsets
reviews.reason: In the set-theoretic representation of categorical inference, universal affirmative premises are encoded as subset inclusion relations and chained by transitivity to test whether a proposed inclusion must hold.
reviews.counterexample: One can track an individual witness and apply universal premises directly in quantified predicate language without translating predicates into sets and subsets.

reviews.scope: represent existential overlap or disjointness by intersections
reviews.reason: When modeling quantified statements with sets, existential overlap is expressed as a nonempty intersection and universal exclusion as an empty intersection between the corresponding predicate extension sets.
reviews.counterexample: Direct reasoning with existential witnesses and universal contrapositives in quantified logic checks entailment without formulating set intersections.

reviews.scope: represent negative class membership using complements
reviews.reason: The set-model approach represents negated predicates and universal exclusion premises by taking complements inside a chosen universe of discourse so that inclusion and disjointness can be analyzed algebraically.
reviews.counterexample: A direct predicate-logic proof or finite witness countermodel handles negation on individual elements without constructing set complements.

reviews.scope: original rational-expression domain and numerator zeros
reviews.reason: Solving any rational inequality requires identifying where the algebraic fraction is defined and where it equals zero, ensuring original denominator zeros remain excluded even under weak inequalities or cancellation.

reviews.scope: strict and weak inequality meanings and solution sets
reviews.reason: Selecting positive or negative sign intervals and deciding whether numerator zeros belong to the final solution set require understanding strict versus weak inequality relations and solution-set representation.

reviews.scope: solve quadratic numerator and denominator sign cases
reviews.reason: When a rational inequality with quadratic numerator or denominator is solved by splitting into same-sign or opposite-sign cases, each case requires solving quadratic inequalities in one variable.
reviews.counterexample: Factoring numerator and denominator completely into linear factors and testing interval signs on a single sign chart bypasses solving separate quadratic inequalities.

reviews.scope: intersect simultaneous sign conditions within each case
reviews.reason: Decomposing a quotient inequality into paired sign cases requires intersecting the solution intervals of simultaneous numerator and denominator inequalities within each branch before taking the union of branches.
reviews.counterexample: A unified factor sign chart or number-line interval test determines the quotient sign directly on each subinterval without solving systems of inequalities.

reviews.scope: finite iterates defined by an initial value and recursion
reviews.reason: Giving a well-defined meaning to a nested radical or infinite power tower requires specifying its initial truncation and the recurrence relation that generates successive finite iterates.

reviews.scope: passing limits through continuous elementary functions
reviews.reason: Evaluating elementary function limits and continuous extensions builds intuition for passing a convergent sequence limit through a continuous recursion map, though sequence convergence must be justified separately.
reviews.counterexample: Monotone bounded sequence convergence and fixed-point algebra on the recurrence equation establish the limit without punctured-domain algebraic limit simplification.

reviews.scope: solve a nested-radical fixed-point equation
reviews.reason: For infinitely nested radicals, finding the candidate limit from the fixed-point equation requires squaring a radical equation and enforcing nonnegativity and domain constraints to reject extraneous roots.
reviews.counterexample: Positive power-tower problems lead to exponential fixed-point equations and do not involve solving radical equations.

reviews.scope: positive power-tower iteration as an exponential map
reviews.reason: Analyzing a right-associated positive power tower requires understanding positive-base exponentiation and exponential function behavior to formulate the iterate recursion and evaluate candidate fixed points.
reviews.counterexample: Infinitely nested radical expressions use root extraction recurrences and quadratic fixed-point equations without exponential functions.

reviews.scope: place-value scaling under multiplication by powers of ten
reviews.reason: Converting a repeating decimal to an exact fraction requires understanding how shifting the decimal point multiplies or divides a value by powers of ten to align repeating blocks.

reviews.scope: solve the linear shift-and-subtract equation
reviews.reason: In the shift-and-subtract method, setting a variable for the repeating decimal and subtracting shifted multiples produces a one-variable linear equation solved by combining like terms and dividing.
reviews.counterexample: Expressing the repeating decimal tail as a convergent infinite geometric series and applying the sum formula yields the fraction without solving a linear equation.

reviews.scope: sum the repeated decimal block as a geometric series
reviews.reason: The series method decomposes the repeating decimal tail into powers of one-tenth with common ratio less than one in magnitude and applies the convergent infinite geometric series sum formula.
reviews.counterexample: Multiplying the decimal by appropriate powers of ten and subtracting to cancel the infinite repeating tail converts the number to a fraction without infinite series formulas.

reviews.scope: reduce the resulting rational fraction to lowest terms
reviews.reason: Both shift-subtraction and geometric-series conversion typically produce denominators such as 99 or 990 that share common factors with the numerator, requiring fraction reduction to obtain lowest terms.
